fact: The IGC study says the revenue management systems in Blantyre, Lilongwe and Mzuzu consolidated scattered Excel and Word registers of property and business owners, with their payments and liabilities, into one database per city, used to produce demand notices and business licences.

The IGC study says Zomba's revenue management system, installed in 2017 with about 15 POS devices, covers market rates, bus depots and parking only, not city rates or business licences, and that the POS use lapsed from 2019 and was only slowly reinstated from 2021.

The IGC study says each of the four city councils runs its own cloud-hosted revenue system from a different vendor, with no national push or coordination, and that planned integration with the IFMIS, banks and mobile money had not been achieved in any of the four cities, so receipts were uploaded separately to both systems.

The IGC study says revenue management systems were introduced in all four of Malawi's city councils (Blantyre, Lilongwe, Mzuzu, Zomba) since 2017, out of 35 local governments (28 districts, 4 cities, 3 municipal councils); it names none in the other 31.

The IGC study says the city systems are supplied under revenue-share contracts: Blantyre build-transfer-operate by Technobrain for 7 years at 15-20% of the relevant revenue, Lilongwe by Nitel for 5 years at 20%, Mzuzu by Technobrain at 15% (markets only), Zomba by Nitel at 3% (markets only), and that changes to back-end data needed the vendor.

The IGC study says the cities have no comprehensive IT strategy and adopted piecemeal systems, and that there was no overarching national push to adopt them; the document is dated August 2023 and gives no date for this finding beyond the research period.
The IGC study says Mzuzu's earlier REMOP property-rates system, introduced in 2013, was provided by donors under a donor-funded programme.
